pillar_reactions.evidence: The rep led with the joints-versus-muscle argument for a beginner — 'if you haven't been working out, your joints and everything, they're gonna collapse at some point, because muscles are growing faster than joints can adapt' — and the prospect interrupted to agree and then extended the argument himself: 'Yeah, exactly that is the thing that I liked, and the reason why I'm here... the thing I saw in that video was like, it's not only, it's like the mixture of sport and workout. Like, it includes movement... it's something that attacks both angles, not only muscle building, but also flexibility.' He also volunteered his prior preference for calisthenics over gyms as a reason this fits. Unambiguously enthusiastic: he tied the pillar to his own goal without being asked, and the sit-to-stand longevity point landed on top of the father-versus-father-in-law thread he had raised earlier.

Pre-conceded as with every other call in this batch — 'nutrition for you is, from what I'm hearing, already [good]... Trevor probably would mainly fine-tune it.' The standard three variables were delivered (what, when, how much; whole foods; a 10-to-8-hour window) with one sensible personalisation: 'For you, probably it's going to be fine-tuned to your specific needs, because as you said, it's difficult for you to gain muscle. So you can probably eat more and you don't have to keep this strict window.' The prospect gave no reaction at all. Scored accepted rather than clarifying because he asked nothing — which is itself notable, since he had walked in with an active nutrition problem he had self-diagnosed: a hard-gainer on a mostly vegetarian diet who believes he must 'double my protein intake', has just started whey, and has just bought creatine. The pillar as scripted is built around not overeating; this prospect's entire problem is the opposite, and the rep's adjustment was a single sentence.

The rep positioned it correctly as the pillar that matters for this specific prospect — 'third part, I think for you, it's going to be crucial. Because you've been trying to start that and you gave up a few times' — and closed with 'when work gets crazy, and it probably will, or motivation dips, you don't fall off like before.' Immediate agreement: 'I agree.' The enthusiasm arrived properly later, unprompted, in the middle of the price objection, when he volunteered his own vivid case for it: 'I work out, I do a push-up, and I'm thinking, like, damn, I have no idea if I did this push-up the right way or not... and if there was somebody standing right next to me telling me like, hey, no, those legs aren't straight, I'd be correcting them, but I don't have it — and I don't have the money to pay it, so so be it.' He also endorsed the differentiation directly: 'Definitely. I definitely agree. And in programming everything.' This is the central finding of the call: full, articulate, volunteered agreement on the value of the accountability pillar, and zero willingness to pay for it. The pillar was not the problem.

anchors.raw: if we compare them, they're both at home. Amazing. They're both easy and quick. Amazing. They both give you more strength. Amazing. One of them also gives you the mobility and that sounds super amazing. One of them also has somebody that's following you up... Super amazing. That sounds amazing. But one of them is free. That's, I think, more amazing than the rest. I'm going to be honest.
anchors.note: The decisive anchor, and the most articulate statement of it anywhere in the corpus. Note what makes it different from the known $29/month case: the substitute costs nothing, it is currently working — three weeks in, the longest streak of his life — and the prospect conceded every point of Primal's superiority before choosing it anyway. Price is being compared against zero, so no amount of value-stacking closes the gap. The rep also weakened his own position by agreeing the content is free ('Everything, all the knowledge, everything, it's on YouTube'), which the prospect immediately took as concession: 'Yeah, that's exactly my point.'

anchors.raw: 6k is like five and a half k more than I could ever think of. Like I just bought the protein today and I thought like damn this is a good investment if I really want to do this — and that was like 25 dollars.
anchors.note: The most useful number in the call. His internal reference price for a fitness purchase is $25, and $25 already felt like a considered investment. The offer is 240x his anchor. This is not a negotiation gap, it is a category mismatch, and it was discoverable in Phase 2 with a single question about what he currently spends on his health. Nobody asked.

anchors.raw: I'm paying no rent and spending all my money on bolognesa pasta so yeah my current cash is zero... I have the exact cash I need to pay my credit cards, which I've used to buy the tickets to fly to Italy. So yeah, zero.
anchors.note: Absolute rather than relative constraint. Cash is zero and the credit lines are already committed to the flights for the trip he is currently on. This is the point at which a financing partner becomes the only mechanism, and the rep offered one — but never asked available versus used credit, so nobody on the call knew whether financing was even reachable.

anchors.raw: I obviously spend more money on other things. More than that, I pay my rent, but I need a house. And I pay Netflix, because I love movies. And I pay delicious food. I'm in Italy right now. And I'm eating amazingly. And I spend a lot of money on food. But that's a priority for me. My physique... not that much.
anchors.competitor: Netflix, restaurant food in Italy, a three-month family trip through Europe
anchors.note: Cuts both ways and the rep played it correctly. It undercuts price because it proves the money constraint is really a priority constraint — he found budget for a three-month European trip and eats out lavishly. But the rep converted it into the disqualification rather than the close, drawing out the admission himself: 'So it turns out, it's not a priority for you.' 'Not that much. Exactly.' That is the honest read, and it is also the moment the deal formally died.

anchors.raw: wanting to starting to learn how to bike, and after two seconds, going and buying a mountain bike that's 6k. I would never do that. I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k, but not now.
anchors.note: A demand for a cheaper rung on the ladder, expressed as a fully reasoned purchasing philosophy rather than a stall. Given three prior abandonments at two weeks, his refusal to buy a premium tool before proving he will use it is objectively sound reasoning, and the rep had no product to answer it with.

anchors.raw: As I told you before, I don't know if specifically Trevor, but like you said, if there's...
anchors.note: Recorded as an anchor because it is what was in his head at the moment of the price: coaching in general, not this coach. He was sold on the category of accountability and never sold on the person. Forty minutes of pitch produced no reason to believe Trevor specifically, which matters for a premium price — and it slipped past because the rep treated the sentence as an isolation yes and moved on.

anchors.raw: The reason why I've been training the last three weeks and I'm planning to do it by myself is because I don't have the budget to pay somebody to follow me and do all this that you're saying.
anchors.note: Recorded deliberately as a null result: this call contains no supportive anchor at all. No partner already enrolled, no history of paying for coaching of any kind, no prior premium purchase in the category, no referral. Every anchor in the room pushed against the price. In a corpus where closes tend to have at least one supportive anchor, its complete absence here is the cleanest predictor of the outcome and worth carrying into the rollup.

unmet_demand.want: A low-cost way to prove the commitment before committing capital — a cheap first rung between free YouTube content and $6,000. 'I would first go and buy a small, used bicycle... and then after a year, then I'll see if I'm prepared to spend 6k, but not now.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing was offered between free and $6,000. No guide, no short trial, no single paid onboarding or form-check session, no deposit that holds a price. The rep's only intermediate instrument was a third-party financing partner, which changes the payment schedule but not the commitment size, and the prospect rejected it on exactly that basis: 'for 6k? No. Because it's not something I would ever pay 6k for.' A low-priced guide product does exist in the business — it appears in other calls in this corpus — and it was never mentioned here.

unmet_demand.want: A reason to believe this coach specifically rather than coaching in general — 'I don't know if specifically Trevor.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Nothing on the call established Trevor's credentials, results, client outcomes or differentiation. He was referred to throughout as the mechanism ('Trevor will prepare', 'you get his direct number') and never as a reason. The prospect had found him via a single Instagram video, was not a follower, and could not name him at the start of the call. The programme almost certainly has the proof; none of it was deployed, which is a positioning failure rather than a capability limit.

unmet_demand.want: Hypertrophy nutrition for a lifelong hard-gainer eating a mostly vegetarian diet — he had already self-diagnosed that he must 'double my protein intake', had started whey that day and bought creatine.
unmet_demand.why_unmet: The nutrition pillar as delivered is built around restraint — clean whole foods, a 10-to-8-hour eating window, 'how much takes care of itself' — which is a weight-management frame. His problem is the inverse, and it is complicated by a household that is meat-free. The rep's entire adjustment was one sentence: 'you can probably eat more and you don't have to keep this strict window.' Whether the programme actually delivers vegetarian-constrained muscle-gain nutrition is genuinely unknown from this call and should be checked with a human rather than assumed either way.

unmet_demand.want: Live form correction for a complete beginner — 'if there was somebody standing right next to me telling me like, hey, no, those legs aren't straight, I'd be correcting them, but I don't have it.'
unmet_demand.why_unmet: Recorded as served, not as a gap, and included here only because it is the clearest positive signal in the call: the offer does exactly this via video submission and Trevor's feedback loop, the rep explained it, and the prospect agreed it was valuable. It failed on price alone. Logging it so the rollup does not mistake this loss for a product deficiency — the product matched the want and the wallet did not.
